replying_to: Replying to A Spectral Perspective of Neural Networks Robustness to Label Noise

content.title: Interesting direction, limited analysis
content.review:
Summary: the paper discusses the effect of a form of spectral regularization on the Jacobians of a model as a way of handling overfitting to noisy examples. The authors show that the Fourier coefficients grow as O(1/k^2) where k is the frequency index. Also, they show that the regularization term can be upper-bounded by L2 norm or Frobenius norm of the weights. The analysis is performed for a univariate function approximation.

Review: the authors adopt an interesting take on analyzing spectral normalization and WD. However, the analysis is quite limited and in some cases, lacks rigorousness. Also, it is not clear how the analysis generalizes to a wider class of multivariate models. 

1) The analysis is performed for a univariate function approximation and therefore, upperbounding the integral in Eq (4) becomes trivial. It is not clear how this argument generalizes to the multivariate case.
2) The argument that the noise usually has high frequency components is not convincing and requires some mathematical proof. Currently, it looks like the authors are trying to match the noise model to the analysis, not the other way around.
3) How good is the O(1/k^2) bound in practice? This requires some careful analysis and experimentation. 
4) The proof of Proposition 1 (Eq (15)) heavily depends on the assumption that the inputs are uniformly spaces (which is not a reasonable assumption). The authors mention that generalization to the random case can be done by non-orthogonal subsampled Fourier frames, but this is not immediately obvious!
5) Proof of Proposition 4 is unclear and might have some errors: "We get equation 10 by simply observing that ...". Eq (9) has an equality constraint while Eq (38) is upperbounding the requirement of Proposition 2 by this constraint. This doesn't seem correct.

Minor: A later work (Amid et al. 2019a) generalizes the GCE loss (Zhang and Sabuncu 2018) by introducing two temperatures t1 and t2 which recovers GCE when t1 = q and t2 = 1. A more recent work, called the bi-tempered loss (Amid et al. 2019b) extends these methods by introducing a proper (unbiased) generalization of the CE loss and is shown to be extremely effective in reducing the effect of noisy examples. Please consider referencing these papers as part of third approach for handling noise in the Related Work section.

Additional references:

(Amid et al. 2019a) Amid et al. "Two-temperature logistic regression based on the Tsallis divergence." In The 22nd International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, 2019.

(Amid et al. 2019b) Amid et al. "Robust bi-tempered logistic loss based on Bregman divergences." In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2019.

content.title: Extended the analysis to multivariate and clarified all other comments in the paper
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed comments. We have modified the paper according to all of them. 
We provide here point by point answer to the comments raised by the reviewer 

1. Following the reviewer’s comment, we have extended all the analysis to the multivariate case. 

2.  Indeed, we assume in our work that label noise has high frequencies. Yet, this is not an assumption that we try to match to the model but rather something that we observe empirically. Notice how the Jacobian of the network increases significantly when label noise is added to the training. Also, notice in the new table that we added (Table 4), how the spectral norm of the network increases when label noise is added. Both of these measures are proven to be related to having high frequencies in the mapping. Thus, our analysis with the empirical observations shows that indeed label noise is related to high frequencies, which may explain the success of spectral normalization to increase robustness to this type of noise. 

3. In the 1-dimensional setting, we can indeed see that we get a fast decay when we train the network. Yet, we do not dwell about it because of the following reasons: a. It is impractical to apply the Jacobian regularization on all network inputs. Therefore, this bound serves as a motivation for the spectral normalization that has a bound of 1/k but imposes a regularization on all inputs 
b. Presenting the Fourier representation is practical only for low dimensional inputs. We show such an example in Figure 1. Yet, we prefer to focus our experiments on real data, where we show that frequencies decay but in an indirect way through calculating the Jacobian and spectral norm of the network.
Notice that we added a new table in the experiment section that demonstrates that indeed the spectral norm of the network increases when the noise increases. 

4. We agree that this is not obvious and therefore defer this to future work. We have clarified this in the text. 
Notice also that Proposition 4, which directly addresses the spectral noise does not require the uniform sampling assumption. Thus, we believe that the current results provide sufficient motivation for using the spectral norm for label noise, which our empirical results validate.

5. We have modified the text there to clarify why this is correct. We hope that it is clearer now. 

Minor comments: Thanks for the references. We have added them to the related work.

content.title: Needs more work and motivation.
content.review:
The authors propose a spectral normalization approach to improve robustness of neural networks under mistaken labels. For the theoretical portion, first they examine a regularization approach based on the first derivative of the neural network, and show that there is a decay of the higher frequency components, at least when training size goes to infinity. They then propose to bound the derivative by the network’s weights. They then empirically draw relationships between the noise in the training data and the smoothness of the learned network. They then went back to the regularization and considered the constrained optimization formulation, and came up with (shrinkage) expressions of the global optimal, and then showed again that in the constrained weights setting this corresponds to decay in the higher frequency components. 
This paper considers neural networks from a Fourier/spectral perspective, which is an interesting trend in the recent theoretical literature. However, there are several comments and issues that the authors should address. 
The authors should comment/write more clearly on what their motivation is? In the abstract they claimed “This work uses recent developments in the analysis of neural networks function space to provide an explanation for their robustness”,  but in the actual paper they are mainly analyzing a regularization approach of neural networks, with little analysis of the function space of the neural network itself. It seems like they are really analyzing how a regularization approach improves robustness, rather than explaining why neural networks themselves are robust to noise. Perhaps they could either 1. Tone down their claims on explaining robustness of neural networks via functional analysis or alternatively 2. Actually more explicitly link their regularization approach to function spaces that are relevant to Fourier etc, say Sobolev spaces etc. 
The authors need to address where the substantial novelty comes from. Spectral normalization/looking Fourier components has already been looked at quite extensively in the literature (which the authors have cited). Their proposed way of bounding derivatives by weights is based on a lemma by Sokolic et al.  In the formulation in proposition 3 they are basically doing a slightly modified L2 regularization on the frequencies. The constrained approach is a simple consequence of adding the regularization term (the dual), and the resulting thresholded/shrinkage expression is well known within the optimization literature. The authors should state and argue clearly where the substantial novelty/big idea is. 
It appears to me that the results in some of the propositions are not sufficient to justify their clams and is quite repetitive (they are essentially saying the same thing). In proposition 1, they show that the Fourier coefficients decay in the first derivative regularization scheme. Then In proposition 2, they use weights as a proxy upper bound for the derivative. How good is this approximation? Is the upper bound tight? Are there better approximations? Then in proposition 3, they looked at the constrained version (dual) of proposition 1 (essentially l2 regularization), and in proposition 4 they showed that in the constrained version with weight normalization, the Fourier coefficients decay. It appears that propositions 3 and 4 is an extension of proposition 1, which says that if you penalize the derivative (or normalize the weights) fourier coefficients decay. To summarize the propositions, this is basically a modified low pass filter, written in different optimization formulations. It is well known in signal processing that low-pass filters attenuate high-frequency noises, so again I am not sure where the novelty is, and how an analysis of a regularization method (already proposed previously in the literature) could substantiate the authors claim of explaining robustness to noises of neural networks (without the regularization)
The authors should address certain assumptions in their theoretical analysis, and link the experiments to the theory in a better way. First, they consider a univariate output setup  in their analysis with smoothness assumptions, but in their experiments, they are doing classification (presumably not univariate output). Second, in the experiments where they looked at CIFAR-10 accuracy of different regularization methods, it is unclear how this links to their theoretical claims. They did not look at SN alone (they looked at SN + l2), and also SN has been proposed in the literature before. They should link this to the theory better. 

Overall, the idea is interesting, but the authors need to justify where the novelty and substantial contribution comes from, needs to motivate the paper more clearly, should consolidate some of their propositions, and should better link the experiments to theory.

content.title: Paper novelty explanation and additional experiments
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed comments. We have modified the paper according to all of them. We provide here a response to the reviewer's claims.

"Function space should be tone down": We thank the reviewer for this comment. We have toned down the claims: We have modified the abstract and added a paragraph at the end of the introduction that emphasizes the contribution of the paper in the context of regularization. 

"Paper novelty": The novelties of the work can be summarized by these three main steps, where to the best of our knowledge each of them is novel by itself (and was not presented before):
a.	Showing that regularization on the network Jacobian either directly or through spectral normalization reduces the high frequency in the learned network mapping. Notice that now the analysis in Proposition 1 also covers the multivariate case (which is novel to the best of our knowledge). 
b.	Showing empirically that adding noise to the training data: (i) adds high frequencies to the learned mapping in the one-dimensional case, where we can practically draw the spectrum; and (ii) increases the Jacobian of the network and its spectral norm in the high-dimensional setting. Both of these steps support our assumption that noise adds high frequencies to the learned mapping. We borrow the intuition from signal processing, where random noise (usually) lies in all the spectrum compared to the signal that mainly resides in the low frequencies). 
c.	Demonstrating that indeed, using the spectral normalization increases the network robustness to noise. We show that the same holds for Jacobian regularization but more minorly as it does not regularize all the spectrum as spectral normalization does. 

"The tightness of spectral norm regularization": Moreover, we have added a discussion about the tightness of the spectral norm upper bound that we use after proposition 4. 

"Low pass interpretation" - notice that we have extended our analysis to the multivariate case. Thus, it goes beyond the simple use of existing 1-dimensional results. 

"Link between experiments and theory" - To better link the theory to practice, we have extended all the theory to the multivariate case (in the input). We believe that this provides a stronger connection to theory. We also added results to SN alone, where improvement is observed as well. The reason that we show mainly SN+l2 is that it practically leads to better results.

content.title: Review
content.review:
This paper studied the connection between smoothness regulation and the robustness of neural networks to random noise. The connection is that a smooth function has fast decay fourier coefficient, and random noise in the label mostly contribute to the high order fourier coefficient, thus forcing the neural net to be smooth can make it robust to the random noise in the label. Various techniques can be used to encourage smoothness of the neural net, including weight regulation with spectral norm and early stopping. Real and synthetic data experiments are conducted to verify the theoretical findings.

Weakness/questions:
1. Novelty of the theoretical findings. I am not sure about the novelty of the theoretical findings. Random noise has high order fourier coefficients and the fact that Lipchitz coefficient of a neural net can be bounded by the product of the spectral norms of the parameter matrices seem well known.
2. About early stopping. The authors argue that early stopping makes the network robust since low frequency components are learnt first. However, I can’t find an explanation of that. At the end of page 4, it reads “In addition, we conclude that a network trained with WD first learns the low frequencies.” It is not clear to me how this conclusion arises.
3. Experimental findings are concerning to me. Table 2 and Table 3 seem to suggest that even with spectral constraints/regularization, the accuracy of the network still decreases quite a lot, and in fact regularization only improves the accuracy by ~2% compared to no regularization at all.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Extension to multivariate case and novelty
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed comments. We have modified the paper according to all of them. We provide here point by point answer to the comments raised by the reviewer

1. We would be happy to get a reference to this claim. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to show the impact of noise on the spectral norm of the network and the Jacobian and relate it to the high frequencies induced by the noise. Moreover, while the relationship between the Jacobian and the product of spectral norms is known (as we clearly admit in the paper – in Proposition 2 we put in brackets the reference to Sokolic et al. 2017), the connection to the spectrum of the network (e.g., Proposition 1) was not shown before as far as we know. Notice also that we have extended our analysis to the multivariate case. 

2. From proposition 1 – a network trained with a penalty on its first derivative has a spectrum decay of 1/||k||^2, such that the penalty increases with ||k||. As a larger penalty is imposed on the higher frequencies, it is expected that during the training process the network will first learn the lower frequencies. This conclusion is indicated and explained after proposition 1.
Thus, using proposition 2, we expect that a network trained with WD will have similar behavior. We have updated the text to explain this better. 

3. First notice that the vanilla network that we compare to already uses early stopping, which improves already the baseline results. Moreover, we applied SN in a very simple fashion to isolate its improvement. Clearly, by combining it with other techniques (such as the popular mixup) we get additional improvement. This shows that our method improves network robustness to noise both when trained alone and with other techniques.

content.title: Review of A Spectral Perspective of Neural Networks Robustness to Label Noise
content.review:
This work has two main contributions. First, the authors analyze an univariate neural network trained to fit a set of points generated by a ground-truth function that can be fit perfectly, under the assumption that the network can be optimized to reach the minimum of a least squares cost function. The analysis shows that bounding the spectral norm of the neural network weights attenuates high frequencies. Second, the authors show that spectral normalization provides a modest increase in performance in the presence of label noise.

Quality: 

The theory in the paper relates spectral normalization to the Fourier coefficient of a 1D function learned via regression by a neural network under the assumptions that it attains a global minimum. This setting is very far from the problem of performing classification on high-dimensional data with a neural network when the labels are noisy. In fact, the theory does not even consider  noisy data. The authors provide some heuristic discussion connecting smoothness to robustness to label noise, but that is all. In addition, the significance of the numerical results is not clear, since the authors do not combine their approach with state-of-the-art methods. 

Clarity: 

The paper is not written clearly. The authors keep referring to noisy labels when explaining their theory, but there are no noisy labels in the actual theoretical results.

Originality: 

I am unsure to what extents the connection between spectral normalization and smoothness is novel. 

Significance:

As explained above, the theory does not seem very relevant to the main topic of the paper. For the numerical results the authors do not consider state-of-the-art methods. The potential impact is therefore quite limited. 

Pros:

The numerical results show that in some cases spectral normalization can help with label noise.

Cons:

Disconnect between theory and topic of the paper. Limited computational experiments.

I would like to thank the authors for their response, but I don't agree that they have addressed my concerns.

Thank you for your comments. We have modified the paper according to all of them. We provide here a response to the reviewer's claims.

"This setting is very far from the problem of performing classification on high-dimensional data": First, we have extended the analysis to a multivariate setting. Moreover, we would like to emphasize the connection we make between theory and practice.  The paper makes the following logical steps:
a.	Showing that regularization on the network Jacobian either directly or through spectral normalization reduces the high frequency in the learned network mapping
b.	Showing empirically that adding noise to the training data: (i) adds high frequencies to the learned mapping in the one-dimensional case, where we can practically draw the spectrum; and (ii) increases the Jacobian of the network and its spectral norm in the high-dimensional setting. Both of these steps support our assumption that noise adds high frequencies to the learned mapping (Borrowing the intuition from signal processing, this is to be expected as usually random noise lies in all the spectrum compared to the signal that usually lies mainly in the low frequencies). 
c.	Demonstrating that indeed, using spectral normalization increases the network robustness to noise. We show that the same holds for Jacobian regularization but more minorly as it does not regularize all the spectrum as spectral normalization does. 
We have updated the paper to emphasize this. 

"Combining with state-of-the-art" - 1. When considering regularization based techniques mixup is one of the leading approaches. Clearly, one may add other more sophisticated methodologies but we focus in this paper on regularization based approaches. 
2. We focus mainly on applying SN in a very simple fashion to isolate its improvement and emphasize it.
